svg.aria-label: Diagram: private services access in Google Cloud and the VPC Network Peering that managed services create on your behalf; reaching a VPC-hosted service such as Cloud SQL or Memorystore means Google provisions a VPC network exclusively for you and joins it to yours with a VPC Network Peering connection, so the service answers on an internal IPv4 address and external addresses are neither required nor used; you allocate one or more IP ranges that are then reserved exclusively for the producer and cannot be used for subnets or as destinations of custom static routes, and the producer picks a subnet from that range, typically a slash twenty-nine to slash twenty-four, which you can neither select nor modify, with a new subnet created for each region; only one consumer VPC network may hold the private connection to a given instance, with Network Connectivity Center producer spokes, Shared VPC, or hybrid connectivity as the ways to widen reach; and the hybrid trap, where the peering exchanges subnet routes only, the producer network already carries a default route to the internet that takes precedence so exporting your own default route is ignored, and the remedy is to export a custom route with a more specific destination
svg.title: Private services access: a peering you did not create, and the routes it does not carry
svg.text: Provision a Cloud SQL instance and you have created a VPC Network Peering. Probably unknowingly.
Which means #81’s non-transitivity now applies to your database.
What actually gets built
“This private connection is established using a VPC NETWORK PEERING connection.”
Google creates a VPC network EXCLUSIVELY FOR YOU, containing only your resources, and peers it
with yours. The instance answers on an INTERNAL IPv4 address.
External addresses on your VMs are neither required nor used.
The allocated range: you give up address space, and lose control of what sits in it
You allocate one or more ranges — in the worked example, 10.240.0.0/16, which is 65,536 addresses.
That range is RESERVED EXCLUSIVELY FOR THE PRODUCER and CANNOT be used for other resources —
not subnets, not destinations of custom static routes.
The producer then carves a subnet out of it, typically /29 to /24. You CANNOT SELECT OR MODIFY
that subnet’s range. A service instance in another region means another subnet.
Size the allocation for every service and every region you will ever add, not for today.
The hybrid trap, in three sentences
1. The peering exchanges SUBNET ROUTES ONLY — so by default on-premises hosts CANNOT reach
the producer’s network. Your VPN and Interconnect routes do not exist on their side.
2. The producer’s network already carries a DEFAULT ROUTE (0.0.0.0/0) to the internet.
3. So EXPORTING YOUR OWN DEFAULT ROUTE IS IGNORED — theirs takes precedence. Export a CUSTOM
ROUTE WITH A MORE SPECIFIC DESTINATION instead.
The obvious fix silently does nothing. The working fix is one word narrower.
One connection per instance — and three ways to widen it
“Only ONE service consumer VPC network can create a private connection to a given managed
service instance.”
• NCC — make it reachable from other spokes via a producer VPC spoke
• SHARED VPC — allocate the range and create the connection in the HOST project
• HYBRID — the custom-route export above. Or ask whether the producer offers Private Service Connect.
Who uses this: the list is longer than people expect
AlloyDB • Apigee • Backup and DR • Cloud Build • Cloud IDS • Cloud SQL • Cloud TPU • Filestore
Managed Lustre • NetApp Volumes • VMware Engine • Looker • Memorystore • Vertex AI • AI Platform
One carries its own caveat on the page: Cloud SQL does NOT support DNS peering.
What you still own
You can create FIREWALL RULES IN YOUR VPC NETWORK to control access to the producer’s network —
so egress control to your own database is yours, even though the subnet is not.
And the sentence to read before assuming Google has you covered: “When you use private services access as a
service consumer, you are SOLELY RESPONSIBLE for securing your VPC networks and all resources and data
available on them.”
